gui.semiconductor-lab.refiner.max: Now: %s (limit of zone refining). Add a dopant to make n/p-type
gui.semiconductor-lab.refiner.ready: Now: %s - transistor grade. Add a dopant, or refine to 10N
gui.semiconductor-lab.refiner.doping: Zone leveling: spreading dopant evenly through %s germanium
gui.semiconductor-lab.refiner.no_boat: Put a graphite boat in the middle
gui.semiconductor-lab.refiner.need_power: No power: the HF oscillator is off
gui.semiconductor-lab.refiner.clay_cap: Clay boat stops at 9N. 10N: synthetic boat
gui.semiconductor-lab.refiner.route_cap: Sulfate-route Ge stops at 9N. 10N needs GeCl4
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite_boat.not: Molten germanium does not react with graphite. Silicon does (forms SiC) - which is why Chapter 2 needs a different method.
message.semiconductor-lab.refiner.not_ge: Only germanium can be zone-refined here. Put in reduced or refined germanium.
message.semiconductor-lab.refiner.max_pu: Already 11N - zone refining cannot go further.
message.semiconductor-lab.refiner.empty: The furnace is empty. Right-click with germanium to start.
item.semiconductor-lab.refined_germanium: Purity is about the inside of the crystal. The surface gets dirty from your hands and air at once - real labs etch it off with acid (CP-4) right before use. Not yet in the game.
Made by zone leveling: dopant is added to the molten zone so it spreads evenly. Mixing solids would not work.
Made by zone leveling: dopant is added to the molten zone so it spreads evenly. Mixing solids would not work.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite_boat.not: The old 19th-century kind: cheap, but clay impurities seep into the germanium, so it only gets you to 9N.

Clay-graphite crucibles (natural graphite bonded with clay) were the standard for melting metals in the 19th century. For semiconductors the clay (aluminium, iron, alkali metals) is the problem - Bell Labs used high-purity synthetic graphite.
item.semiconductor-lab.synthetic_graphit: A boat carved from very clean man-made graphite. Germanium gets all the way to 10N.
Goes in the middle slot of the zone refining furnace and is not used up. With this boat germanium refines to 10N (the clay-graphite boat stops at 9N).
Molten germanium does not wet or react with graphite, so a clean graphite boat adds almost nothing to the bar. Pfann's zone refiners used high-purity graphite boats inside a quartz tube.

Omitted: real boats are machined on a lathe/mill from a graphite block, then purified further by baking in chlorine or freon gas at about 2500 C (metal impurities leave as volatile chlorides). Here 3 synthetic graphite are shaped at the crafting table.
block.semiconductor-lab.zone_refining_fu: Melt only a thin slice of the bar and slide it along: the dirt follows the melt to the end.

Left: germanium (max 8). Middle: graphite boat (not used up; clay-graphite = up to 9N, synthetic = up to 10N). Right: dopant. Runs on electricity: the built-in HF oscillator draws 3 kW (stops without power). 30 s per pass.

The HF oscillator drives the copper coil; the alternating magnetic field induces currents in the germanium itself, so only the part inside the coil melts. The boat and the quartz tube stay cool enough not to contaminate it. (The same principle as an induction cooktop. This furnace is the [3-14] induction furnace of the tech tree.)
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite_boat.not: In Pfann's zone refining (Bell Labs, 1952) the germanium bar rode in a graphite boat through a quartz tube. Molten germanium barely wets graphite, so the bar comes out cleanly after it freezes.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite_boat_bla: A graphite boat before firing. Still soft.
Made from 3 graphite and clay. Fire it in a furnace (or the electric furnace) to get a clay-graphite boat.
Clay (kaolinite, Al2Si2O5(OH)4) loses its bound water at around 500 °C and hardens. The clay acts as the glue that holds the graphite grains together.

Clay-graphite crucibles were mass-produced in the 19th century for melting steel and brass; the Morgan company, founded in London in 1856, started out making them. Graphite conducts heat well and is hard for molten metal to wet.
item.semiconductor-lab.junction_transist: A 1950s transistor, much sturdier than the point-contact kind.
Fire the unfired part in a furnace. Three of them make a transistor radio.
A p-n-p structure: a thin n-type Ge base between two indium-soaked p-type layers (emitter and collector). A small base current controls a large emitter-to-collector current - amplification.
Developed around 1951 at GE and RCA. Easy to make, it was widely used in 1950s hearing aids and radios, but the base was hard to make thin, so it was poor at high frequencies.
Germanium sandwiched between indium, before firing.
Made from [indium][n-type Ge][indium] + copper. Fire it in a furnace to get an alloy-junction transistor.
At about 500 °C the indium melts and dissolves a little germanium. On cooling the Ge recrystallizes with indium inside it, forming a p-type layer. Doing it from both sides gives p-n-p.
How deep the two indium dots alloy in sets the base width. Controlling both sides at once was hard, so bases could not be made much thinner than 10 to a few tens of µm.
Germanium with a tiny bit of extra electrons.

Ge bonds to its neighbours with 4 electrons. A group-15 phosphorus atom (5 electrons) has one left over, which moves freely and carries current. Even one P atom per hundred million Ge atoms changes the conductivity greatly.
The n stands for negative: the carriers are negatively charged electrons. Early Bell Labs n-type Ge often used antimony or arsenic, but phosphorus is a genuine n-type dopant for Ge too.
Germanium a tiny bit short of electrons.
A group-13 indium atom (3 electrons) leaves one bond missing - a hole. When a neighbouring electron hops in, the hole appears to move, acting just like a moving positive charge.
The p stands for positive. The idea of the hole came from Peierls and Heisenberg around 1929-31, to explain metals whose Hall effect looked as if positive charges were flowing.
item.semiconductor-lab.refined_germanium: Extremely pure germanium, the stuff transistors are made of.

Zone refining: most impurities prefer the liquid to the solid (segregation coefficient k < 1). Sweep the molten zone the same way again and again, the impurities pile up at one end, and that end is cut off.
Invented by William Pfann at Bell Labs in 1952. A few passes brought impurities down to nearly one in ten billion (10N), giving the first material good enough for mass-produced transistors.
item.semiconductor-lab.transistor.note1: The world's first transistor: a small current controls a big one.
item.semiconductor-lab.transistor.note2: Made from 2 gold ingots + n-type germanium + copper.
item.semiconductor-lab.transistor.note3: Two gold contacts, a few tens of µm apart, are pressed onto an n-type Ge slab by a plastic wedge. Holes injected at one (the emitter) strongly change the current at the other (the collector) - the signal was amplified up to about 100 times.
item.semiconductor-lab.transistor.note4: Bardeen and Brattain at Bell Labs got it working on 16 December 1947, demonstrated it on the 23rd and announced it on 30 June 1948. The story goes that gold foil was wrapped round the wedge and slit at the tip with a razor to make the gap (⚠️ details unconfirmed). They shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics with Shockley.
block.semiconductor-lab.zone_refining_fu: For silicon a graphite boat cannot be used (silicon reacts with it to form SiC), so the floating-zone method (around 1953) was developed: the bar stands upright and surface tension alone holds the molten zone.
block.semiconductor-lab.crystal_puller.n: Like cotton candy, it 'pulls' a crystal up out of molten germanium.

Uses 3 kW (built-in HF oscillator). Top left: refined germanium; middle: the seed; bottom left: hydrogen bags (also pulled from an adjacent gas holder). With tungsten wire as the seed, 1 Ge makes a seed crystal (30 s, the wire is used up); with a seed crystal, 4 Ge make a single-crystal ingot (60 s, the seed comes back). Purity and route carry over to the ingot.

A graphite crucible (germanium does not react with carbon) is kept just above Ge's melting point of about 938 °C by HF induction heating. In hydrogen, which prevents oxidation, a seed crystal is dipped into the melt and slowly pulled up while turning. The liquid freezes copying the seed's atomic arrangement, so the whole bar becomes one crystal. Real pull rates are 1-4 cm per hour, at 3-20 turns per minute.

The method itself was found in 1916 by the Pole Jan Czochralski while measuring how fast metal crystals grow (he is said to have dipped his pen into molten tin instead of ink). Teal and Little at Bell Labs used it for semiconductors in 1950. Told that polycrystals were good enough, Teal spent over a year persuading management - and single crystals made transistor performance uniform almost overnight.
gui.semiconductor-lab.crystal_puller.nee: Insert a seed (W wire or seed crystal)
item.semiconductor-lab.germanium_seed_cr: A small piece of germanium with its atoms lined up perfectly - a 'model' for the crystal to copy.
Made in the crystal puller with tungsten wire in the seed slot (the very first one). Used as the seed when pulling single crystals, and not used up.

The first seed comes from grain selection: polycrystal forms on the tip of a thin wire, and pulling it out thin lets only the fastest-growing grain survive. After that, the end of a finished crystal is cut off to seed the next one. The seed's orientation sets the orientation of the whole ingot.

In 1959 W. C. Dash at GE found that necking the crystal down very thin just below the seed, then widening it again, lets defects (dislocations) grow out, giving dislocation-free crystals (Dash necking). Every silicon crystal today still starts from that thin neck.
item.semiconductor-lab.germanium_single_: A bar of germanium that is one single crystal throughout.
From the crystal puller: a seed crystal + 4 refined germanium. Purity and route stay as they were. More uses will come, e.g. the grown-junction transistor [9-10].

A polycrystal is a patchwork of small crystals pointing different ways. Electrons and holes are easily lost at the boundaries (grain boundaries), so properties vary from place to place. A single crystal has no grain boundaries: carriers live longer (long minority-carrier lifetime) and every slice behaves the same.

Teal moved to Texas Instruments in 1952 and in 1954 used crystal pulling to make silicon grown-junction transistors. The single-crystal technique that began with germanium became the doorway to the silicon age.
block.semiconductor-lab.cz_puller.note1: Melts very pure silicon and slowly pulls one huge crystal out of it, like candy floss on a stick.
block.semiconductor-lab.cz_puller.note2: 150 kW (graphite heater). Seed: polysilicon in the seed slot + quartz crucible + argon 1 → silicon seed crystal (60 s). Ingot: seed crystal (kept) + polysilicon 2 + quartz crucible + argon 2 (+ B2O3 for p-type or phosphorus for n-type, or nothing for intrinsic) → silicon single crystal (835 s = 17.4 kWh/kg). Crucibles are used once. Pulls argon from an adjacent gas holder. Real growers add the dopant as small chips of silicon containing a lot of B or P (master alloy).
block.semiconductor-lab.cz_puller.note3: Silicon melts at 1414 °C and reacts with graphite (forming SiC), so the crucible is quartz. The quartz slowly dissolves into the melt, so CZ crystals contain oxygen (about 10^18 atoms per cm³). Argon keeps air out and carries away the SiO that boils off. Boron enters the crystal almost evenly (segregation coefficient about 0.8); phosphorus mostly stays in the melt (about 0.35), so the bottom of an n-type ingot is more strongly doped.
block.semiconductor-lab.cz_puller.note4: Jan Czochralski found the method in 1916 while measuring how fast metals crystallize. Today's ingots are 300 mm across and about 2 m long, weighing a few hundred kilograms. In 1959 Dash showed that pulling a very thin neck first removes the dislocations ⚠️. Most of the world's silicon wafers are made this way.
block.semiconductor-lab.cz_puller.placeh: ⚠️ Approximation: pulling is about 8× faster than real (about 1 mm per minute; the energy matches 17.4 kWh/kg). Argon amount is symbolic (real: tens of mol per kg). The dopant goes in directly as B2O3 / phosphorus; real growers add a master alloy (silicon chips with lots of B or P) ⚠️. Diameter control and oxygen amount are not modelled.
gui.semiconductor-lab.cz_puller.need_see: Put polysilicon or a seed crystal
item.semiconductor-lab.quartz_crucible.n: A glass-like bowl of pure quartz that can hold molten silicon.
Fused quartz ×5 (U shape). Used once per pull in the CZ puller [9-08].
Silicon would react with a graphite crucible and turn into SiC, so silicon is melted in quartz (SiO2). The quartz softens near 1420 °C and slowly dissolves, adding oxygen to the crystal.
Real crucibles crack when the leftover silicon cools and expands, so each one is used for only one pull.
item.semiconductor-lab.quartz_crucible.p: Approximation: real crucibles are made by fusing high-purity quartz sand in a spinning mould with an electric arc; here it is crafted from fused quartz.
item.semiconductor-lab.silicon_seed_crys: A small piece of perfect crystal. The big crystal copies its direction.
Made in the CZ puller from a polysilicon tip. Used again and again (not used up) to grow single crystals.
When you dip the seed into the melt and pull, atoms line up following the seed. Pulling a thin neck first lets only one grain and no dislocations survive.
Real seeds are cut from earlier crystals in a chosen direction (such as <100>), and the direction decides the wafer's surface.
Approximation: the crystal direction is not shown.
item.semiconductor-lab.silicon_single_cr: One giant crystal of silicon. All its atoms line up in the same direction.
From the CZ puller [9-08]: polysilicon 2 → 1 ingot (about 2 kg). Purity comes from the polysilicon; B2O3 makes it p-type, phosphorus n-type. Next it is sliced into wafers [9-12].
In polycrystals, electrons scatter at grain boundaries; in a single crystal every transistor behaves the same. CZ crystals contain oxygen from the quartz crucible.

Boron spreads almost evenly from top to bottom (k ≈ 0.8), but phosphorus piles up toward the bottom (k ≈ 0.35), so an n-type ingot's resistance changes along its length. Oxygen is a weakness, but small oxygen clusters can also trap metal impurities (gettering).
Approximation: 1 ingot ≈ 2 kg; real ingots are a few hundred kg. Uneven doping along the ingot and oxygen are not modelled.
block.semiconductor-lab.wafer_saw.note1: A spinning steel disc with diamonds on its edge slices a silicon crystal into thin plates.
block.semiconductor-lab.wafer_saw.note2: 1 kW (motor). Silicon single crystal 1 → silicon slices 8 (60 s). Purity and dopant pass to the slices. One diamond saw blade lasts 4 ingots.
block.semiconductor-lab.wafer_saw.note3: Silicon is hard and brittle, so it is ground away by diamond, the hardest material. The width of the blade turns into powder (kerf loss), so a good part of the ingot is lost.
block.semiconductor-lab.wafer_saw.note4: In 1954 Bell Labs cut long strips from a crystal to make the first practical solar cells. Later came inner-diameter saws (1970s) and multi-wire saws that cut hundreds of wafers at once (tried around 1980, widespread from the 1990s to the early 2000s ⚠️), which need precision stages.
block.semiconductor-lab.wafer_saw.placeh: Omitted: ⚠️ Power (1 kW), time (60 s), 8 slices per ingot and blade life are game values (no source). Wafer thickness and the powder are not shown.
gui.semiconductor-lab.wafer_saw.need_inp: Needs a crystal and a blade
item.semiconductor-lab.diamond_saw_blade: A steel disc with diamonds stuck around its edge.
Steel ingot + diamond ×4. Used in the wafer saw [9-12]; one blade lasts 4 ingots.
Only something harder than silicon can cut it cleanly. Diamond (pure carbon) is the hardest natural material; the diamonds slowly fall out as the blade wears.
Real blades use many tiny industrial diamonds bonded to the rim, not whole gems.
Approximation: real blades use diamond grit, not whole diamonds.
item.semiconductor-lab.silicon_wafer.not: A thin plate cut from a silicon crystal. Solar cells and chips are made on it.
From the wafer saw [9-12]: 8 per ingot, same purity and dopant as the ingot. Next: diffusion furnace [9-16] to make a p-n junction.
Because the whole slice is one crystal, every part behaves the same. The 1954 solar cells used long strips; today's wafers are round, 300 mm across and under 1 mm thick.
Modern wafers are lapped, etched and mirror-polished [9-13] before use. The 1954 cells did not need a mirror finish.
item.semiconductor-lab.silicon_wafer.pla: Approximation: shape and thickness are not modelled; polishing [9-13] comes later.
block.semiconductor-lab.diffusion_furnac: Bakes silicon slices so that a little boron or phosphorus soaks into their surface.

5 kW. Silicon slices 8 (n-type or p-type) + 1 dopant source of the opposite type → p-n junction slices 8 (120 s). n-type slices take B2O3 (boron makes a thin p-type top, like the 1954 cell); p-type slices take phosphorus. Undoped or same-type slices make no junction, so it will not run. (The real 1954 base was arsenic-doped n-type; the game uses phosphorus, also group V.)

At high temperature, dopant atoms wander slowly from the surface into the solid (diffusion, Fick's law). A thin layer of the other type forms on top, and where it meets the base is the p-n junction, the heart of solar cells and transistors.

In 1954 Fuller diffused boron into arsenic-doped (n-type) silicon to make the first practical solar cell. Earlier cells made with lithium were unstable because the lithium kept moving at room temperature. From 1955, an oxide mask let dopant enter only through chosen windows.

Omitted: ⚠️ Temperature (about 1000 °C), power (5 kW) and time (120 s; real diffusion takes hours) are game values not yet checked against sources. The real 1954 base was arsenic-doped; here phosphorus (also group V) is used because arsenic is not in the game yet. The carrier gas is omitted.
n + B → p-n / p + P → n-p
item.semiconductor-lab.pn_junction_wafer: A silicon slice with a thin layer of the other type on top. Light on it makes electricity.
From the diffusion furnace [9-16]. 8 of them + copper cable make a solar cell [B-12].
At the junction, electrons and holes are pulled apart by a built-in electric field. When light frees an electron, the field pushes it one way and the hole the other: that is a current.
The same p-n junction is inside every diode and transistor. A solar cell is a big, flat diode that faces the sun.
Approximation: junction depth and the thin top layer are not modelled.
block.semiconductor-lab.oxidation_furnac: Bakes silicon slices in oxygen or steam to grow a thin film of glass (SiO2) on their surface.

5 kW. Silicon slices 8 (oxidized slices also work) + 1 bag of oxygen (dry) or 1 water bucket (wet; the empty bucket comes back) → oxidized slices 8 (120 s = one real hour at 1100 °C). Film thickness follows the Deal–Grove equation: dry about 125 nm, wet about 660 nm. 1–8 process wafers with open windows get their windows closed again (redo a wrong etch). Takes oxygen from a gas holder next to it.

Oxygen has to soak through the film already formed to reach the silicon, so the thicker the film, the slower it grows (thickness squared grows with time). Steam passes through the film much faster than oxygen, so wet oxidation makes thick films quickly. Dry oxidation is slow but gives a denser, better film.

In 1955 Frosch and Derick at Bell Labs were diffusing into silicon in hydrogen when the hydrogen caught fire, made steam, and covered the slices with oxide (⚠️ another account blames a leaky tube). The film turned out to block dopants: a mask (published 1957). Germanium's oxide GeO2 dissolves in water and cannot be used as a mask, one reason silicon won.

Omitted: ⚠️ Power (5 kW) and time (120 s = one real hour) are game values. The temperature is fixed at 1100 °C (real furnaces choose 900–1200 °C). Thickness uses values for <111> silicon; crystal orientation, doping level and chlorine-added oxidation are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.oxidized_wafer.no: A silicon slice covered by a thin film of glass (SiO2). Its colour changes with the film thickness.
From the oxidation furnace [9-15]. The tooltip shows the film thickness (nm). Opening windows in this film to let dopant in is the later planar process [9-18].

The colour is light interference: light reflected from the top and bottom of the film reinforces a different colour depending on thickness. Factories guessed thickness by comparing with a colour chart (about 125 nm is blue, about 660 nm near violet).

Silicon protects itself with its own 'rust', which is glass. The SiO2–silicon interface has very few defects, so it later became the insulator under the gate of the MOSFET [9-23], the most-made device in history.
item.semiconductor-lab.oxidized_wafer.pl: Approximation: the film is equally thick over the whole slice. Colours are a rough summary of the colour chart.
block.semiconductor-lab.etch_tank.note1: A lead tank of hydrofluoric acid. It dissolves only the glass film (oxide) on silicon slices.
block.semiconductor-lab.etch_tank.note2: 1 acid per run (the empty bottle pops out on top). Hydrofluoric acid: 1–8 developed process wafers → oxide dissolves only where there is no resist, opening 'windows'; 8 oxidized slices → all oxide stripped. Time depends on film thickness (125 nm about 6 s). Phosphoric acid: 1–8 aluminium-coated, developed wafers → aluminium stays only under the resist and becomes wiring (10 s). Room temperature; no power or fuel.
block.semiconductor-lab.etch_tank.note3: SiO2 + 6HF → H2SiF6 + 2H2O. HF dissolves oxide readily but hardly touches silicon itself (selectivity). When the film is gone, the surface starts to repel water, so you can see when it is done.
block.semiconductor-lab.etch_tank.note4: In 1957 Lathrop and Nall (US Army laboratory) opened holes in oxide, keeping the parts protected by resist. Later factories used buffered HF (BHF), diluted with ammonium fluoride, to keep the etch rate steady. ⚠️ Whether Bell Labs' window opening from 1955 used HF is not confirmed.
block.semiconductor-lab.etch_tank.placeh: Omitted: ⚠️ The etch rate (20 nm per second) is a game value (real diluted HF etches some tens to 100 nm per minute). Sideways etching (undercut) is not modelled. The tank is lead, not polyethylene.
item.semiconductor-lab.process_wafer.not: A silicon wafer getting its mask patterns printed one by one.
Coat resist → expose → develop → etch → diffuse, once per mask. If something goes wrong, strip the resist and try again.
In 1959 Hoerni had the idea of the planar process: keep the oxide and only open windows to diffuse through. The surface stays flat, so many parts can sit side by side and be wired with metal.

Around 1960 an IC took three diffusions (isolation, base, emitter) and one layer of aluminium wiring, just like in the game. The real process first grew an n-type layer as a crystal (epitaxy) ⚠️; the game doesn't have that yet, so it diffuses n-type islands instead.
block.semiconductor-lab.drafting_table.n: A desk for drawing chip patterns on a grid. Draw whatever you like.
Pick a layer, left-click to paint and right-click to erase. The cross-section below shows it from the side. ✂ cuts the chosen layer out as artwork.
1960s ICs were drawn large on grid paper, then red film (rubylith) was cut by hand into artwork and photographically shrunk hundreds of times to make the mask.
The artwork was hundreds of times the chip size and was cut on a big table that reads coordinates (a coordinatograph) ⚠️. Later, computer drawing (CAD) replaced it.
block.semiconductor-lab.drafting_table.p: Approximation: grid sheets and artwork come without materials (really paper and film)
item.semiconductor-lab.layout_sheet.note: A chip pattern drawn at the drafting table, with every layer.
Put it back on the drafting table to keep drawing. Cut each layer out as artwork to make masks.
Layers follow the process order: island (n) → base (p) → emitter (n) → metal contacts → aluminium wiring. A later diffusion is stronger, so overlaps take the later type.
Real designs must keep line widths and gaps (design rules) or the chip fails. In the game one cell is the smallest line.
item.semiconductor-lab.layout_sheet.plac: Approximation: no materials (really large grid paper)
item.semiconductor-lab.rubylith.note1: Red film carrying one layer's pattern.
item.semiconductor-lab.rubylith.note2: Photograph it with the reduction camera to make a photomask.
item.semiconductor-lab.rubylith.note3: Cut and peel the red film and light passes only there. Photographic plates don't see red light, so red prints like black.
item.semiconductor-lab.rubylith.note4: An IC needed several masks, and each one had its own cut artwork. A cutting mistake became a faulty chip.
block.semiconductor-lab.wafer_polisher.n: Presses wafers onto a spinning plate and polishes them like a mirror. It grinds off every circuit layer so you can start over.

1 kW. 1–8 process wafers + 1 abrasive (alumina or rouge) + 1 colloidal silica (the empty glass bottle pops out on top) → wafers with all layers removed (60 s). Each wafer can be reclaimed twice at most.

First hard grit grinds the wafer flat (lapping) and the damaged layer is removed, then colloidal silica polishes it. The silica particles are soft and the alkaline liquid dissolves a little of the silicon surface, so chemistry and mechanics together give a scratch-free mirror.
In 1963 Walsh and Herzog at Monsanto filed a patent for mirror-polishing silicon with colloidal silica (US 3,170,273). It is the ancestor of CMP [9-31], which flattens today's many-layered chips.
block.semiconductor-lab.wafer_polisher.p: Omitted: ⚠️ power and time are game values. Wafer flatness is not modelled yet. Lapping and polishing are one step.
gui.semiconductor-lab.wafer_polisher.nee: Needs wafers, abrasive and colloidal silica
gui.semiconductor-lab.wafer_polisher.rec: Grit to flatten → silica to mirror
block.semiconductor-lab.probe_station.no: A stand for touching a finished chip with needles to see if current flows.
Click the pads on the edge to choose 0 V, 5 V or open; current glows yellow. Press Probe to identify the circuit. A dirty chip leaks current and sometimes works, sometimes not (washing fixes it).
In a real fab, fine needles touch every chip on the wafer to sort good from bad. Bad chips are marked and thrown away later.
Not every chip works. The share of good chips (yield) depends on dust and defects and on chip area (Y ≈ e^(−D·A)).
block.semiconductor-lab.probe_station.pl: Omitted: the measuring power supply (battery) and needle alignment
block.semiconductor-lab.cleaning_bench.n: A tank for washing dirt off wafers with acid between steps, then rinsing with clean water.

1 kW (warms the nitric acid). 1–8 process wafers + 1 nitric acid + 1 hydrofluoric acid + 1 rinse water (distilled, deionised or ultrapure; the 3 empty bottles pop out on top) → wafers cleaned down to dirt 1 (40 s). A little metal remains; to reach 0 use the RCA clean bench. Wafers with resist cannot be cleaned. Dirt builds up by 1 at each etch, strip, diffusion and aluminium step.

Hot nitric acid oxidises and dissolves metal and grease. Hydrofluoric acid removes the thin surface oxide together with the dirt trapped in it. A final rinse in salt-free water leaves no chemicals behind. This is how 1950s plants washed wafers (stage 1).

A trace of invisible sodium or iron makes transistors vary and fail. In 1965 Kern at RCA put together a wash with ammonia water, hydrochloric acid and hydrogen peroxide (the RCA clean), still the basis in factories over 50 years later (stage 2, to come).
block.semiconductor-lab.cleaning_bench.p: Omitted: ⚠️ power and time are game values. Real benches have three tanks in a row. Dirt is a single number (organics, particles and metals are not separated).
item.semiconductor-lab.al_dotted_wafer.n: A p-n junction slice with small aluminium dots on its surface.

In the vacuum evaporator [5-14]: p-n junction slices (p slice with an n top) + 1 aluminium → 1–8. A slice with an n base and p top is refused (aluminium is p-type too, so no junction forms). Bake in a furnace to alloy.
Evaporating through a metal plate with holes (a metal mask) leaves dots only where the holes are: the oldest way, without photoresist.
In silicon, aluminium is a p-type dopant. Dissolving into the n surface, it leaves a thin p layer underneath: the emitter.
item.semiconductor-lab.alloyed_wafer.not: The aluminium dots have been baked into the silicon; under each dot is now a small p layer (emitter).
Al-dotted slice → furnace → 1. Coat with honeycomb (beeswax) to protect only the dots.

Aluminium and silicon melt together at about 577 °C (the eutectic). On cooling, silicon recrystallises with aluminium in it, forming a p layer: p (slice), n (diffused top), p (aluminium) make a pnp transistor.
A diffused base with an alloyed emitter was a common recipe for germanium mesa transistors (1957–58).
item.semiconductor-lab.alloyed_wafer.pla: Approximation: silicon mesas later diffused the emitter as well (2N697 and others). Here the emitter is alloyed aluminium.
item.semiconductor-lab.waxed_wafer.note1: A slice with black wax covering only the dots that will become transistors.
item.semiconductor-lab.waxed_wafer.note2: Alloyed slice + honeycomb (beeswax) → 1 (crafting). In the etching tank with mixed acid, the unwaxed silicon dissolves and only plateaus (mesas) around the dots remain.
item.semiconductor-lab.waxed_wafer.note3: Wax does not dissolve in acid, so it was long used to etch patterns into glass with HF: the 'mask' before photoresist.
item.semiconductor-lab.waxed_wafer.note4: Real plants dropped picein or black (petroleum) wax onto each dot by hand, so few transistors fitted on a slice.
item.semiconductor-lab.waxed_wafer.place: Approximation: beeswax is used (real practice often used black petroleum wax). Dissolving the wax off afterwards is omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.mesa_wafer.note1: Only the transistor parts are left standing, like little table-top plateaus.
item.semiconductor-lab.mesa_wafer.note2: Waxed slice + mixed acid (etching tank [9-06], 10 s) → 1–8. With 2 gold nuggets and 1 iron nugget at the crafting table → 4 mesa transistors.
item.semiconductor-lab.mesa_wafer.note3: On the side of each plateau the p-n junction edge is exposed. Moisture or ions there let current leak.
item.semiconductor-lab.mesa_wafer.note4: 'Mesa' is Spanish for table: named after the flat-topped, steep-sided plateaus of the American West.
item.semiconductor-lab.mesa_transistor.n: A transistor shaped like a plateau (mesa). Its junction is exposed, so it gets worse while you carry it.
Mesa slice + 2 gold nuggets (gold wires) + 1 iron nugget (header) → 4. Current gain β starts at 40 and drops by 1 every minute in your inventory, by 5 in rain or water; at 0 it stops working.
Made by diffusion, mesa transistors were fast (high frequencies); Bell Labs, TI and Fairchild built them in 1957–58. But the junction lay bare on the surface and drifted with dirt and moisture.
In 1959 Hoerni at Fairchild devised the planar process [9-18], keeping the junction hidden under oxide. Protected junctions could be laid out in large numbers on a flat surface, and the IC was born.
item.semiconductor-lab.mesa_transistor.p: Omitted: ⚠️ The rate of decline is a game value (really days to months depending on humidity and temperature). Sealing in a metal can with dry nitrogen (hermetic packaging) is not available yet.
block.semiconductor-lab.fz_puller.note1: Makes a single crystal by melting just part of a silicon rod, with no crucible. The molten part floats in the air.
block.semiconductor-lab.fz_puller.note2: 20 kW (induction heating). 2 polysilicon + silicon seed crystal (kept) + 2 argon (topped up from a gas holder next to it) + dopant (optional) → 1 silicon single crystal (300 s). Unlike CZ, no quartz crucible is used up. The crystal has very little oxygen (about 0.05 ppma).
block.semiconductor-lab.fz_puller.note3: Melting part of an upright rod with a coil, the molten zone is held between the solid parts by surface tension. Moving the zone along leaves single crystal behind. Nothing touches the melt, so no oxygen or dirt dissolves in from a crucible.
block.semiconductor-lab.fz_puller.note4: In 1952 Theuerer at Bell Labs turned zone refining upright (patent filed December 1952, granted 1962); Keck and Golay (US Army) in 1953 and Emeis at Siemens in 1953–54 did it independently. Low-oxygen, high-resistivity silicon is used for power devices and radiation detectors. ⚠️ FZ is older than the Siemens process (1956 on) because it first used silicon made by reducing silicon tetrachloride with zinc (DuPont). The game uses Siemens polysilicon.
block.semiconductor-lab.fz_puller.placeh: Omitted: ⚠️ power and time are game values. That FZ struggles to grow large-diameter crystals (big wafers are mostly CZ) is not modelled.
block.semiconductor-lab.spin_coater.note: Spins wafers fast to spread photoresist into a thin, even layer.

500 W. 1–8 oxidized slices or process wafers + 1 positive resist (the empty bottle pops out on top) → resist-coated wafers (20 s). Spoiled resist cannot be used. Includes warming to drive off the solvent (prebake).

Liquid dropped in the centre spreads outward under the force of thousands of turns per minute and the excess flies off. The faster the spin, the thinner the film (about 1 µm): like spinning pizza dough.
Spin coating spread in the 1960s. ⚠️ The exact start date is not yet checked. Almost every liquid coating on wafers is still applied this way.
block.semiconductor-lab.spin_coater.plac: Omitted: ⚠️ power and time are game values. Film thickness and spin speed are not modelled.
A tank that dissolves used photoresist off wafers with hot acid.

500 W. 1–8 process wafers with resist + 1 sulfuric acid + 1 hydrogen peroxide (the 2 empty bottles pop out on top) → wafers with the resist removed (20 s). Used after opening windows, and for rework when an exposure went wrong.

Strong sulfuric acid mixed with hydrogen peroxide becomes a fiercely oxidising liquid (containing Caro's acid) that turns organic matter like resist into carbon dioxide and water. It hardly attacks oxide, silicon or aluminium wiring.

It eats organic matter so violently that it is nicknamed 'piranha solution'. Mixing releases a lot of heat, and accidents where organic solvents got in and it erupted are why fabs handle it in a fixed order with dedicated containers. ⚠️ When fabs began using it is not yet checked (Caro's acid: Caro, 1898).
Omitted: ⚠️ power and time are game values. Later oxygen-plasma stripping (ashing) is not available yet.
block.semiconductor-lab.mask_aligner.not: A machine that lays a mask on a resist-coated wafer and prints the pattern with mercury lamp light.

4 steel + compound microscope + 2 lead screws + mercury lamp tube + copper cable. 500 W, 10 s. Coated wafer + photomask -> exposed wafer. The button switches the gap: contact is sharp but wears the mask by one use per wafer (10 uses), 20 um proximity spares the mask but blurs a little, 80 um blurs too much to print. A stage screw (lead screw or ball screw) in the small top slot lines later masks up with the earlier layers (overlay: hand 20 um, lead screw 10 um, ball screw 5-1 um).
In 1955-57 Andrus and Bond at Bell Labs and Lathrop and Nall of the US Army applied photoengraving to making transistors. It began with contact printing: the mask pressed onto the wafer at 1:1.

In contact the mask and wafer rub, adding dirt and scratches, so masks were replaced after a few uses. Proximity printing keeps the mask longer but light bends around the edges (diffraction): blur ~ sqrt(wavelength x gap). Projection printing through a lens ([7-19]) removed both weaknesses.
block.semiconductor-lab.mask_aligner.pla: Approximation: looking at the alignment marks is automatic. Overlay = the largest of stage feed, microscope resolution and floor vibration (game values). The blur formula is simplified (sqrt(lambda x gap)).
gui.semiconductor-lab.mask_aligner.mask_: Mask has too few uses left
Dips exposed wafers in developer so the mask pattern appears in the resist.

300 W (hot plate). 1–8 exposed process wafers + 1 developer → developed wafers (20 s). Positive resist uses dilute NaOH developer (the empty bottle pops out on top) and dissolves where light hit; negative resist uses xylene and dissolves where light did not hit. The wrong developer does nothing. A hot plate then hardens the remaining resist (postbake).
Just like developing photographic film, the circuit pattern appears. The hardened resist then protects the film underneath during HF or phosphoric acid etching.
Opening windows by developing resist began in 1955–57 with Andrus and Bond at Bell Labs and Lathrop and Nall at the US Army, using Kodak's KPR resist. ⚠️ When postbaking began is not yet checked.

Omitted: ⚠️ power and time are game values. The rinse water is not modelled. Negative resist is developed in xylene rather than KPR's own developer (⚠️ the real KPR developer was a mixture of organic solvents).
item.semiconductor-lab.diamond_scribe.no: Hold a finished wafer in the other hand and use: scratch a grid and snap it into chips.
A diamond point scratches a shallow line along the crystal; bending the wafer breaks it cleanly along the line, like cutting glass. One wafer gives 8 chips; sometimes one chips off.
Around 1960 the first ICs were separated this way: scribe with diamond, then roll or press the wafer to break it. Later a thin saw blade coated with diamond (the dicing saw) cut straight through.

Silicon breaks most easily along its {111} planes, so the scribe lines follow the crystal directions marked by the wafer's flat. ⚠️ The year and the chip count per wafer are game simplifications (a 1-inch wafer held tens to about a hundred dies).
item.semiconductor-lab.diamond_scribe.ho: Hold a process wafer in the other hand
item.semiconductor-lab.diamond_scribe.no: Finish the wafer first (aluminium wiring done, resist stripped)
item.semiconductor-lab.chip.note1: One small piece cut from the wafer. Put it on the probe station to test it.
item.semiconductor-lab.chip.note2: Every chip from one wafer has the same circuit, because the same masks were printed over the whole wafer.
item.semiconductor-lab.chip.note3: The first ICs were a few millimetres across. Next the chip is bonded with thin gold wires and sealed in a package (later nodes).
item.semiconductor-lab.chip.note4: In industry 'die' is the word for one chip (plural dice). The share of good dice per wafer is the yield, which decides the cost of every chip.
block.semiconductor-lab.dicing_saw.note1: Cuts a finished wafer into chips with a spinning diamond blade. Fewer chips break than when you snap them by hand.
block.semiconductor-lab.dicing_saw.note2: Wafer + diamond blade + ball screw (the stage, not used up) + 1.5 kW for 10 s -> 8 chips. Chance one breaks: 4% / 2% / 1% by ball-screw grade (hand scribing: 10%).
block.semiconductor-lab.dicing_saw.note3: A thin disc with diamond grit spins very fast under running water and cuts straight grooves; a precise stage moves the wafer. Saws replaced scribe-and-break as chips grew and wafers got thicker. ⚠️ the year it became common (late 1960s-70s) is not confirmed.
block.semiconductor-lab.dicing_saw.note4: The cut (kerf) is only a few tens of micrometres wide, so little silicon is lost. Today the wafer is first stuck on tape so the chips do not scatter. ⚠️ power, time and break chances are game values.
item.semiconductor-lab.diamond_blade.not: A thin metal disc with diamond grit. Put it in the dicing saw.
Diamond grit held in bronze (a metal bond). It wears a little with every wafer: 32 wafers per blade.
Blades are only about 20-50 µm thick. Metal-bonded (bronze or nickel) and resin-bonded blades are used. ⚠️ the bronze bond and the wear are game simplifications.
Diamond is the hardest material, so it can cut silicon (and sapphire, glass) cleanly; the grit size sets how smooth the cut edge is.
block.semiconductor-lab.rca_bench.note1: Washes wafers in two liquids, ammonia water or hydrochloric acid mixed with hydrogen peroxide. The basis of how fabs clean today.
block.semiconductor-lab.rca_bench.note2: 1.5 kW (warms the liquids to about 75 °C). 1–8 process wafers + 1 ammonia water + 1 hydrochloric acid + 2 hydrogen peroxide + 1 deionised or ultrapure water (empty bottles pop out on top) → wafers with dirt 0 (40 s). Wafers with resist cannot be cleaned.
block.semiconductor-lab.rca_bench.note3: SC-1 (ammonia water : peroxide : water = 1:1:5, about 75 °C) slightly oxidises and dissolves the surface, lifting off organic dirt and tiny particles. SC-2 (hydrochloric acid : peroxide : water = 1:1:6) dissolves metals such as iron and sodium. Each step is followed by a deionised water rinse.
block.semiconductor-lab.rca_bench.note4: Werner Kern at RCA put it together in 1965 and published it in 1970; over 50 years later it is still the basis of cleaning in leading fabs. In the game, stage 1 (nitric and HF) leaves dirt 1 (metals) while RCA brings it to 0.
block.semiconductor-lab.rca_bench.placeh: Omitted: ⚠️ power and time are game values. SC-1, SC-2 and the rinses are one step. Dirt is a single number (SC-1's organics and particles and SC-2's metals are not separated).
gui.semiconductor-lab.rca_bench.need_inp: Needs wafers, NH3, HCl, 2 H2O2, DI water
gui.semiconductor-lab.probe_station.resu: Probe to check the challenge too
Set pads: 0 V, 5 V, inputs and outputs
gui.semiconductor-lab.drafting_table.sym: Symbols on. Click one to look inside
item.semiconductor-lab.stamp.note1: A circuit you found, ready to press again and again on the drafting table.
item.semiconductor-lab.stamp.note2: Solve a challenge at the probe station and you get its stamp. Put it in the drafting table's stamp slot and left-click the grid.
item.semiconductor-lab.stamp.note3: Press the square button to see pressed stamps as symbols; click a symbol to look inside it. Designers did the same: draw transistors once, reuse them as symbols, then build bigger blocks from the symbols.
item.semiconductor-lab.stamp.note4: This is abstraction (hierarchical design): every symbol still stands for real mask shapes, and the probe always judges the shapes, never the symbol.
block.semiconductor-lab.wafer_prober.not: Tests every chip on a finished wafer automatically and marks the bad ones with ink. Only good chips come out when you dice it.
Wafer + ball-screw stage (not used up) + 500 W, 0.5 s per chip. A chip is good if it behaves the same as a clean chip when its leakage varies (dirt makes bad chips).

Fine tungsten needles on a probe card touch each chip's pads while a precise stage steps from chip to chip. The probe station tests one chip by hand and shows the currents; the prober only says good or bad, but tests the whole wafer fast.

Testing before dicing saves the cost of packaging bad chips. The share of good chips is the yield, roughly Y = e^(-D x A) (defect density x chip area). ⚠️ the year of the first automatic probers (1960s) and the times here are not confirmed / game values.
block.semiconductor-lab.stepper.note1: A machine that shrinks the mask pattern with a lens and prints it chip by chip across the wafer.
block.semiconductor-lab.stepper.note2: Mask aligner + 6 steel + motor + copper cable. 1.5 kW. Load a coated wafer, a mask, a projection lens and a stage screw, then press 'Step one chip' four times to finish a wafer (stage 1: stepping by hand). It prints grid 36, finer than contact printing's grid 16 (silver masks stop at 24, so it needs a chrome mask). The mask is never touched, so it does not wear.
block.semiconductor-lab.stepper.note3: In 1978 GCA in the USA released the DSW, starting exposure that shrinks the mask and prints one chip at a time (step and repeat). In the 1980s Nikon and Canon steppers spread through fabs worldwide.
block.semiconductor-lab.stepper.note4: Resolution CD = k1 x lambda / NA. Because the mask is made larger, its dust and errors print smaller. Later came the scanner, sweeping mask and wafer together under a narrow slit of light. Semiconductor history is the history of 'shorter light, finer lines'.
block.semiconductor-lab.stepper.placehol: Approximation: stage 1 steps by hand (real steppers step under computer control; automatic stepping comes with [10-15]). The 1978 DSW reduced 10x (5x here).
gui.semiconductor-lab.stepper.lens_wrong: Lens does not suit this light
item.semiconductor-lab.chip_header.note1: A metal base with leads, for mounting a chip.
item.semiconductor-lab.chip_header.note2: Crafting: 1 steel + 1 soda-lime glass + 1 copper wire → 4. The leads are sealed into the base with glass (airtight). Chips are mounted and wired in the wire bonder [9-33].
item.semiconductor-lab.chip_header.note3: The gaps around the leads are filled with molten glass (glass-to-metal seal), so moisture cannot get in once a metal can is fitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.chip_header.note4: 1960s ICs came in the same round metal cans (TO-5) as transistors. ⚠️ Real leads use an alloy that expands like glass (Kovar).
item.semiconductor-lab.chip_header.place: Approximation: the lead alloy is represented by copper wire (really Kovar and similar).
item.semiconductor-lab.bonded_chip.note1: A chip whose pads are joined to the header leads by fine gold wires. Still bare, so it needs sealing.
item.semiconductor-lab.bonded_chip.note2: Made in the wire bonder [9-33] (keeps the chip's contents). Sealing [9-34] in a metal can or epoxy finishes it.
item.semiconductor-lab.bonded_chip.note3: The gold wires are pressed onto the chip's aluminium pads with heat and pressure (thermocompression). There is one wire per pad.
item.semiconductor-lab.bonded_chip.note4: Today's bonders join more than 20 wires per second automatically.
block.semiconductor-lab.wire_bonder.note: Joins a chip to its leads with gold wire finer than a hair.

200 W (heats the stage). 1–8 chips + gold bonding wire (as many per chip as it has pads) + headers (one per chip) → bonded chips (15 s). Pads are wiring that reaches the chip edge; the NOT example has 4. Chips without pads cannot be bonded.
On a heated stage, pressing the end of the gold wire onto a pad makes gold and aluminium stick (thermocompression). The wire is led to the lead, pressed again and cut.
Thermocompression bonding was devised at Bell Labs around 1957 (⚠️ year not checked). Ultrasonic bonding was added later.
block.semiconductor-lab.wire_bonder.plac: Omitted: ⚠️ power and time are game values. Wire loop shapes and ultrasonic bonding are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.can_cap.note1: A small steel can that goes over a chip.
item.semiconductor-lab.can_cap.note2: Crafting: 1 steel → 8. In the package sealer [9-34] it is fitted over a bonded chip, filled with dry nitrogen and welded.
item.semiconductor-lab.can_cap.note3: Filling the can with dry nitrogen keeps moisture off the chip surface. Transistors and early ICs came in these round cans (TO-5, TO-18 and others).
item.semiconductor-lab.can_cap.note4: The rim of the can and header is joined in an instant with a large current (resistance welding).
item.semiconductor-lab.can_packaged_chip: An IC sealed in a metal can with dry nitrogen. Resists moisture.
Made in the package sealer [9-34] from a bonded chip + can cap + nitrogen. Keeps the chip's contents (which circuit it is).
Early-1960s ICs had leads coming out of round metal cans just like transistors; the Apollo Guidance Computer's ICs started in this form too.
Hermetic cans are costly and heavy but very reliable, so they are still used in space and military equipment.
item.semiconductor-lab.plastic_packaged_: An IC wrapped in a black epoxy body: the familiar 'centipede'.
Made in the package sealer [9-34] from bonded chips + epoxy molding compound (1 per 4 chips). Keeps the chip's contents.
Epoxy compound is pressed into a heated mould around the chip (transfer molding): cheaper than cans and easy to mass-produce. Two rows of leads make a DIP (dual in-line package).

Fairchild introduced the DIP in 1964 (first in ceramic). Plastic DIPs spread from the late 1960s, and calculator and PC boards filled with these black centipedes. ⚠️ The year plastic spread is not checked.
block.semiconductor-lab.package_sealer.n: Seals bonded chips inside a metal can or an epoxy body.
500 W. 1–8 bonded chips + can caps (one each) + 1 bag of nitrogen → metal-can ICs; or 1–8 bonded chips + epoxy molding compound (1 per 4 chips) → plastic ICs (20 s). Keeps the chips' contents.
Moisture or sodium on the chip surface changes its behaviour; enclosing it protects it. Cans are filled with nitrogen and welded; epoxy is pressed into a mould at about 175 °C and cured.
Early transistors and ICs were sealed in metal cans and glass. From the late 1960s cheap epoxy plastic packages (DIP and others) took over. ⚠️ Years not checked.
block.semiconductor-lab.package_sealer.p: Omitted: ⚠️ power and time are game values. Lead trimming and forming and post-seal testing are not modelled.
gui.semiconductor-lab.package_sealer.nee: Needs chips and a can or epoxy
item.semiconductor-lab.cw_multiplier.not: Rectifiers and capacitors arranged like a ladder to multiply a voltage many times.
Crafting: 4 Leyden jars + 2 rectifiers + 2 steel + 1 copper cable → 1. With an accelerator tube it becomes the accelerator of the ion implanter [9-28] (tens to hundreds of kilovolts).
Each AC cycle charges a capacitor and passes it on to the next stage, so the voltage stacks up with the number of stages. Greinacher at the University of Bern devised the circuit in 1920.

In 1932 Cockcroft and Walton in Cambridge used it to reach hundreds of kilovolts and changed lithium nuclei with protons (1951 Nobel Prize in Physics). Such voltages spark through air and can electrocute people who merely come close, so the equipment is fenced and earthed.
item.semiconductor-lab.cw_multiplier.pla: Approximation: a part item; stage count and voltage are not modelled.
A vacuum tube of stacked glass and metal rings. Inside, ions are pushed faster by high voltage.
Crafting: 6 soda-lime glass + 3 steel → 1. With a Cockcroft–Walton multiplier it becomes the accelerator of the ion implanter [9-28].

With slightly different voltages on each metal ring, an ion gets a push at every ring and speeds up. The glass insulates the rings, and the inside is kept at high vacuum so ions do not hit air molecules.

At the same time Lawrence in the US built the cyclotron, accelerating particles round and round in an electromagnet (1930–31, 1939 Nobel Prize in Physics). Accelerators now also treat cancer and make hospital tracers. Fast ions hitting metal give off X-rays, so accelerators are shielded.
Approximation: a part item; length and vacuum level are not modelled.
block.semiconductor-lab.ion_implanter.no: Turns dopant atoms into ions, speeds them up with high voltage and shoots them into wafers.

5 kW. 1–8 process wafers (with developed resist or oxide windows) + 1 dopant source (B2O3 = p-type, phosphorus = n-type) → implanted wafers (30 s). Works only when a vacuum chamber next to it is at 0.01 Pa or below. Implanting alone does nothing until annealing [9-29].

An ion source ionises the dopant, a mass-analysing electromagnet picks only the wanted ion (¹¹B⁺, ³¹P⁺), and the accelerator's high voltage drives it in. Unlike diffusion, windows stay open, ions do not spread sideways, and dose and depth can be set precisely.

Shockley filed the patent in 1954 and implantation became a production step in the 1960s–70s; every fab relies on it today. High voltage can electrocute and fast ions give off X-rays, so implanters are enclosed and shielded. Real ion-source gases, boron trifluoride and phosphine, are highly toxic and their cylinders are kept in monitored cabinets.
block.semiconductor-lab.ion_implanter.pl: Omitted: ⚠️ power and time are game values. Solid sources stand in for the source gases (BF3, PH3). Dose is only recorded; depth is not modelled.
gui.semiconductor-lab.ion_implanter.need: Needs wafers and a dopant source
block.semiconductor-lab.anneal_furnace.n: Heats wafers after ion implantation to heal the damage. Until then, the implanted atoms do nothing.

3 kW. 1–8 implanted wafers + 1 nitrogen or argon → annealed wafers (20 s). Takes nitrogen/argon from an adjacent gas holder. No wafers with resist (strip it first). Wafers without implants do not change.

Implanted ions knock silicon atoms out of place and sit in the gaps themselves. Around 1000 °C the atoms re-order (annealing) and dopants move onto lattice sites where they carry current (activation). Nitrogen or argon keeps the surface from oxidising.

The same idea as annealing iron. Since the 1980s, rapid thermal annealing (RTA) heats wafers for only seconds with lamps, because long furnace heating lets the dopants spread from where they were placed. ⚠️ Furnace temperature and time are typical values.
block.semiconductor-lab.anneal_furnace.p: Omitted: ⚠️ power and time are game values (a real furnace takes about 30 min). No lamp RTA, furnace only. Dopant spreading by heat is not modelled.
block.semiconductor-lab.sputter.note1: Argon ions hit a metal target and the knocked-out atoms settle on the wafer. It also coats the sides of steps.
block.semiconductor-lab.sputter.note2: 5 kW. 1–8 process wafers + 1 aluminium (target wear) + 1 argon → wafers coated with Al (20 s). Works only when a vacuum chamber next to it is at 0.01 Pa or below. Takes argon from an adjacent gas holder. Then, as after evaporation, resist and phosphoric acid turn the film into wiring.
block.semiconductor-lab.sputter.note3: A high voltage across low-pressure argon makes a glow discharge; Ar⁺ ions hit the target and knock atoms out (atomic billiards). Atoms arrive from many directions, so steps cast less shadow than in evaporation. A magnet behind the target traps electrons (magnetron). W, Mo, Ti and alloys can be deposited too.
block.semiconductor-lab.sputter.note4: In 1852 Grove recorded that a discharge tube's cathode wore away and coated the glass. The nuisance became a production tool with the magnetron in the 1970s. High voltage can electrocute, so the system is enclosed.
block.semiconductor-lab.sputter.placehol: Omitted: ⚠️ power and time are game values. Al target only. Better step coverage is only recorded; the circuit is the same as with evaporation (for yield later). Argon pressure during the discharge (~0.5 Pa) is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.carbon_tetrafluor: A gas of carbon with four fluorines. It hardly reacts, except in a discharge, where it releases fluorine.
Fluorination reactor: 1 graphite + 1 fluorine cylinder → 8 bags. Gas for the dry etcher.
C + 2F2 → CF4. The C–F bond is very strong: CF4 does not burn and is of low toxicity. Broken up in a plasma it gives F, which turns SiO2 into gaseous SiF4.
A very long-lived greenhouse gas (about 6,500 times CO2, lasting 50,000 years). Fabs destroy it before release. ⚠️ Figures from IPCC reports.
Omitted: ⚠️ amounts are game values. Industrial CF4 is also made from HF and chlorocarbons.
block.semiconductor-lab.fluorination_rea: Burns carbon in fluorine to make carbon tetrafluoride.
500 W (cooling and control). 1 graphite (or synthetic graphite) + 1 fluorine cylinder → 8 CF4 + empty cylinder (10 s).
Fluorine attacks almost everything, so the reactor is nickel, protected by a fluoride skin. The gas is fed slowly with cooling.
Moissan, who first isolated fluorine in 1886, recorded carbon burning in it. Fluorine work has many accidents and is done in monitored rooms.
Omitted: ⚠️ amount (8 bags per cylinder) and power are game values.
block.semiconductor-lab.dry_etcher.note1: Etches oxide with a discharge (plasma). Unlike liquid HF it only cuts straight down.
block.semiconductor-lab.dry_etcher.note2: 3 kW. 1–8 wafers with developed resist + 1 CF4 → wafers with windows (15 s). Works only when a vacuum chamber next to it is at 0.1 Pa or below. Strip the resist afterwards.
block.semiconductor-lab.dry_etcher.note3: A radio-frequency discharge breaks CF4 into F, which turns SiO2 into gaseous SiF4. The wafer electrode charges negative, so ions strike from straight above and etch only downward (anisotropic: reactive ion etching, RIE).
block.semiconductor-lab.dry_etcher.note4: From the 1970s. Liquids dissolve sideways as much as down, so lines below about 2–3 µm widen and merge. Every fine line in today's chips is dry-etched.
block.semiconductor-lab.dry_etcher.place: Omitted: ⚠️ in game, on grids of 36 or finer (from the g-line stepper) wet windows widen by one cell; dry ones do not. Power and time are game values. Added O2 and discharge pressure are omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnesium_silicid: Bluish crystals made by heating magnesium with silicon. Acid turns it into silane.
Silane generator: 2 magnesium + 1 metallurgical silicon → this. React with 4 hydrochloric acid to fill a silane cylinder.
2Mg + Si → Mg2Si. With acid: Mg2Si + 4HCl → SiH4 + 2MgCl2.
In 1857 Wöhler and Buff made silane (a silicon hydride) for the first time this way. It also reacts slowly with water.
item.semiconductor-lab.silane_cylinder.n: A gas of silicon and hydrogen (SiH4) that catches fire by itself in air. Raw material for CVD films.
Silane generator: 1 magnesium silicide + 4 hydrochloric acid + empty cylinder → this. In the CVD furnace it reacts with oxygen to make the interlayer film (SiO2).
SiH4. At about 400 °C: SiH4 + O2 → SiO2 + 2H2O. Low enough that aluminium does not melt, so it insulates over the wiring.

Pyrophoric (GHS: flame, gas under pressure). Fabs keep cylinders in enclosures with leak monitors and purge lines before opening them. ⚠️ Industrial silane comes from SiHCl3 disproportionation or SiCl4 hydrogenation.
item.semiconductor-lab.silane_cylinder.p: Omitted: ⚠️ the Mg2Si-acid route turns only about 25% of the Si into silane, mixed with disilane etc. Amount per cylinder is a game value.
block.semiconductor-lab.silane_generator: Makes silane gas from magnesium and silicon. What you put in picks the reaction.
1 kW, 10 s each. ① 2 magnesium + 1 metallurgical silicon → magnesium silicide ② 1 magnesium silicide + 4 hydrochloric acid + empty cylinder → silane cylinder (acid bottles pop out on top).
① heats the two without air into an alloy. ② breaks it with acid and fills the gas into a cylinder.
Silane burns on contact with air, so the unit is purged before opening (a gas with many accidents). The magnesium chloride solution is discarded.
Omitted: ⚠️ amounts, power and time are game values. Magnesium chloride is not kept (discarded).
block.semiconductor-lab.cvd_furnace.note: Grows a film on wafers from reacting gases. Covers the first wiring layer with insulation.

2 kW. 1–8 wafers with patterned first metal + 1 silane cylinder + 1 oxygen → wafers with an interlayer film + empty cylinder (20 s). Oxygen comes from an adjacent gas holder. Then via windows (resist → etch) → second Al → etch gives the second wiring layer (METAL2).

SiH4 + O2 → SiO2 + 2H2O at about 400 °C. Thermal oxidation (about 1000 °C) cannot be done over aluminium (melts at 660 °C), so insulation over metal is deposited by CVD. Vias (vertical holes) join the two metal layers.
Two wiring layers let lines cross over each other, so chips get smaller. ⚠️ Two-level metal spread in production around the 1970s (sources being checked). Today's chips have more than ten layers.
block.semiconductor-lab.cvd_furnace.plac: Omitted: ⚠️ power and time are game values. Film thickness, phosphorus doping for reflow (PSG) and planarisation (CMP) are omitted.
block.semiconductor-lab.cmp_polisher.not: Polishes a bumpy wafer surface flat with chemicals and fine particles.

2 kW. 1–8 wafers with an interlayer film + 1 colloidal silica → planarised wafers (30 s, bottle pops out on top). Refuses wafers with resist or a metal film. The particles leave a little dirt (clean it in the cleaning bench).

Alkaline silica slurry flows onto a pad on a rotating platen while the wafer is pressed on it. The chemistry softens the surface and the particles cut the high spots first. Flattening after each layer keeps fine lines in focus (depth of focus DOF = k2·λ/NA²).
IBM began using it in production in the 1980s ⚠️ (date being checked). Like building a skyscraper and levelling each floor before the next. Today it is also essential for copper (damascene) wiring.
block.semiconductor-lab.cmp_polisher.pla: Omitted: ⚠️ real pads are polyurethane foam; nylon felt stands in here. Power and time are game values. Depth-of-focus checks are not in yet (v0.5; steps are only recorded).
